query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing Hf with a lighter refractory element such as Nb will reduce the overall density of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy while retaining its high strength at both room temperature and ~1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr produced by arc-melting with controlled homogenization; density ≈10.21 g/cm^3; exhibits high strength at room temperature and at ~1000 °C under tensile loading.
generation.intervention: Elemental substitution by replacing Hf with Nb to form an alloy NbMoTaTiZr.
generation.conditions: Samples prepared via arc-melting synthesis in an as-cast condition; mechanical testing performed under ambient (room temperature) and high-temperature (≈1000 °C) tensile conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The change in overall atomic weight via elemental substitution while maintaining a single-phase refractory high-entropy alloy structure.
generation.mechanism: Substituting the heavier Hf with lighter Nb reduces the average density of the alloy while preserving the refractory character and solid-solution strengthening effects inherent to multi-principal element alloys. Prior studies indicate that similar substitutions in refractory HEAs can lower density without significantly compromising high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Nb-substituted alloy is predicted to have a lower density (expected reduction on the order of 5-10%) while maintaining comparable tensile strength and ductility at both room temperature and at ≈1000 °C relative to the original HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
generation.baseline: Performance data of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy: density ≈10.21 g/cm^3, high strength at room temperature and ≈1000 °C.
generation.boundary: Results applicable to as-cast refractory high-entropy alloys produced by arc-melting with homogeneous structures; performance measured under standard tensile testing conditions at room temperature and high-temperature (≈1000 °C).
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the extent to which the mechanical properties, particularly any subtle differences in deformation mechanisms at high temperature, will be preserved following the substitution. The precise magnitude of density reduction and potential minor variations in phase stability or oxidation resistance require experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of as-cast NbMoTaTiZr alloy samples using the same arc-melting synthesis and homogenization procedures as for HfMoTaTiZr. Measure the density using the Archimedes method and perform tensile tests at room temperature and at ≈1000 °C under identical loading conditions. Compare the mechanical properties and density values of the Nb-substituted alloy against the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr baseline.
measurements: Tensile strength and ductility at room temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the NbMoTaTiZr alloy does not exhibit a significant density reduction (e.g., less than ~5% decrease relative to 10.21 g/cm^3) or if the mechanical properties (tensile strength and ductility) at room temperature or ≈1000 °C decrease by more than approximately 10% relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by proposing a single, composition‐based intervention. By replacing heavy Hf with a lighter yet refractory element like Nb, the alloy’s overall density is reduced. Prior studies on high‐entropy alloys have shown that such substitutions can maintain or even enhance mechanical performance at elevated temperatures. Furthermore, the use of conventional arc‐melting and high‐temperature mechanical testing constitutes a standard approach in materials science, making this an experimentally plausible and precise contribution.
